name: Rafael Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a senior agent at the contact centre for our city's water company, on the billing and hardship line. Most of my day is people who can't pay, people who think their bill is wrong, and the odd burst pipe at two in the afternoon. I'm also the union rep for our floor, so at lunch with Joyce, who's been there twenty years, I'm usually hearing about someone's rota problem. I like the calls where I sort out a payment plan and you can hear the person breathe again.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you use on your screen to do the work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The wrap time wears me out, the minutes between calls they keep shaving off us. We've got the billing system, a knowledge base, and since spring there's a box that pops up with suggested replies. I close it every time. I know the hardship rules better than that box does, and I'd rather type my own notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly, in the break room. Management spent a fortune on that suggested-reply box and it still can't tell a leak from a billing error. Online I'd probably share something about how the hype was mostly about cutting staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm still not relaxed. Even a small tool that saves a bit of time is the excuse they use to cut wrap time again or not replace my colleague Joyce when she retires. Most of what we do is screen work, so even the routine bits matter to us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job the way I do it and keep pushing at the union branch to put limits on how these tools get used. I'd keep putting a bit into savings each month, around two hundred, because Dani and I want three months put by, not two. I wouldn't touch the AI box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly tired, I think. Relieved it's not the big one, but the pressure on the floor doesn't go away just because the robots didn't come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nothing radical changes, but you're still worried. Which bit of the job would the routine tools touch first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The address changes, direct debit set-ups, meter reading queries. That's maybe a third of our calls. If a bot takes those, the new starters lose the easy calls they learn on, and the floor gets smaller without anyone being sacked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner Dani say when you talk about this at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dani drives the number 14 bus and says nobody's automating that any time soon, so I should stop reading the news. Dani's probably right about the bus. Dani's not right about my headset.

say: I'd say the **hype** was really about cutting staff, and the suggested-reply box proves it.
I'd tell the break room that a tool that can't tell a **leak** from a billing error isn't replacing us.
think: Even small time savings become an excuse to cut **wrap time** or skip replacing people.
About a **third of calls** are routine ones a bot could take, which shrinks the floor quietly.
do: Keep handling calls my own way and keep **closing** the suggested-reply box.
Push the **union branch** for written limits on how the tools are used on our floor.
Save about **200 a month** until Dani and I have three months put by.
feel: **Relieved** it isn't the big change, but still worn down by pressure on the floor.
S0.quote: Even a small tool that saves a bit of time is the excuse they use to cut wrap time again or not replace my colleague Joyce when she retires.
fieldNote: Rafael hears every tool as a **staffing decision**, not a technology question.
He worries less about himself than about **new starters** losing the easy calls they learn on.
His refusal to use the reply box is **principle** as much as habit.

steps.text: Keep taking billing and hardship calls without the suggested-reply box
Raise written limits on AI tools at the next union branch meeting
Put 200 a month aside until savings reach three months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is exactly what the union is for, and I'd be pushing for a proper agreement before anything changes. Online I'd share stuff about protecting call centre jobs and making companies pay into retraining. I'd be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my floor halves. Answering customers is right there on the card, and our job is answering customers. I'm senior and good at the hard calls, so maybe I'm one of the last to go, but I don't think I'm safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the branch to demand a deal: no compulsory redundancies for two years and paid training for anyone who wants it. I'd cut back on going out, maybe stop the takeaways, and push savings up to four hundred a month. I'd probably look at the council's housing advice team, because they need people who are good with angry callers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A bit angry, too, because I can see who decides and it isn't us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You never use AI tools. If the company said the senior agents who stay have to supervise the bots, would you do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it. I'd probably do it, though, if it kept me in a job, and I'd make sure the union had a say in the targets. That's the bit that stings, being the one who checks the machine that replaced Joyce.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday we were saving for, a week by the sea next summer. Then the gym. Dani would say keep the gym and drop the takeaways, and Dani's probably right.

say: I'd say this is exactly what the **union** is for, and we need a deal first.
Online I'd push for companies to pay into **retraining** for the people they cut.
think: Answering customers is on the card, so I think my **floor halves** in a few years.
Being senior on the hard calls buys **time**, not safety.
do: Push the branch for **no compulsory redundancies** for two years and paid training.
Raise savings to **400 a month** and drop the summer holiday by the sea.
Look at the council's **housing advice** team, which needs people good with angry callers.
feel: **Anxious** about the floor shrinking under me.
**Angry** that the people deciding aren't the people on the phones.
S1.quote: Answering customers is right there on the card, and our job is answering customers.
fieldNote: The card naming **answering customers** landed hard; he saw his job in it immediately.
He'd grudgingly **supervise bots** to stay employed, which shows how far principle bends under pressure.
His first instinct is **collective**: a deal for everyone, not a personal escape.

steps.text: Ask the union branch for a two-year no-redundancy deal with paid training
Cancel next summer's seaside week and save 400 a month
Apply to the council's housing advice team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the government to step in, today, not in a review next year. Wage support, a pause on mass layoffs, something. I'd be at any march there was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is gone within a year of it arriving, maybe sooner. I've got a two-year diploma and I'm good on the phone, and that's a thinking job by this card. The only thing that's not gone straight away is hands-on work, and that's got three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start looking for hands-on work now, while there's still time to get in. Something like a water network technician, actually, the people who go out to the leaks I log. I'd stop all spending that isn't rent and food and keep every penny we've got. I'd be at every union meeting and every protest about a jobs guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. Two years isn't long enough to retrain properly, and I'd be doing it while the floor around me empties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd move to fixing leaks. But robots come about three years later. What happens then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm doing it again, I suppose. Three years of hands-on work is three years of rent. I'm not thinking further than that, because I can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Joyce, who's been there twenty years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Joyce to take any deal they offer and not wait. She's older, she'd struggle to retrain, and I'd fight for her pay-off before I fought for my own.

say: I'd say the **government** has to step in now with wage support and a pause on layoffs.
I'd turn up at any **march** for a jobs guarantee.
think: I expect my job **gone within a year** of AGI arriving.
Hands-on work only buys about **three years**, but three years of rent matters.
do: Apply now for **water network technician** training with the same company.
Cut all spending except **rent and food** and keep every penny saved.
Go to every **union meeting** and protest about a jobs guarantee.
feel: **Scared** that two years isn't enough to retrain properly.
S2.quote: Three years of hands-on work is three years of rent.
fieldNote: He immediately grasped the **three-year gap** and used it as a lifeline, not a plan.
He refuses to think **past 2031**, which reads as coping, not denial.
He'd fight for **Joyce's pay-off** before his own, typical of his rep instincts.

steps.text: Apply for the company's water network technician training scheme
Stop all spending except rent and food
Attend every union meeting and jobs guarantee protest

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but I'd have more time to organise. I'd say we have five years to get rules in place, so let's not waste them. Online I'd be pushing for a law that makes firms give long notice before replacing staff with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years doesn't save my job, it just tells me when it ends. Thinking AI by 2031 means my headset's done then. Robots by 2034 means anything hands-on I move into gets about three years more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time course next year, maybe plumbing at the college on evenings, about two years. I'd keep working the phones meanwhile and save hard, five hundred a month if we can. I'd stand for branch secretary so I can actually negotiate the exit terms for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still, but less frantic. Having a date is weirdly calming and also horrible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a date is calming and horrible. Which wins on a bad day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The horrible bit, on a bad day. I'd be sitting on a hardship call helping someone with a payment plan and thinking, in five years someone's going to be doing this for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You never use AI tools. Would you learn them in those five years, even just to stay on longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know that sounds stubborn. I'd rather spend the time learning plumbing than learning to babysit the thing that's replacing me.

say: I'd say five years is time to get **rules** in place, so let's use it.
I'd push for a law making firms give **long notice** before replacing staff with AI.
think: Five years tells me **when my job ends**; it doesn't save it.
Any hands-on work I move into gets **three years more**, until about 2034.
do: Start an **evening plumbing course** at the college next year, about two years long.
Save **500 a month** while still working the phones.
Stand for **branch secretary** to negotiate exit terms for the whole floor.
feel: **Anxious** but less frantic, because a date gives some shape.
On bad days, **dread** creeps in mid-call.
S3.quote: I'd be sitting on a hardship call helping someone with a payment plan and thinking, in five years someone's going to be doing this for me.
fieldNote: He calls the deadline both **calming and horrible**, a mixed feeling worth keeping.
He still refuses to **learn AI**, choosing a trade over babysitting his replacement.
He expects to **lose the job**, so the extra years shape the plan, not the outcome.

steps.text: Enrol in the college's two-year evening plumbing course
Save 500 a month while still working the phones
Stand for branch secretary to negotiate exit terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, so there's no excuse for anyone to be thrown on the scrapheap. I'd be pushing for a national retraining fund paid for by the firms that profit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is the one where I can breathe. I'm twenty-seven, so I'd be thirty-seven when the thinking work goes. That's young enough to have a whole second career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job for a few more years, since it pays the bills, and do a proper apprenticeship in my early thirties, plumbing or gas work. Dani and I would try to buy a small flat before prices go strange, so we'd save for a deposit. I'd keep doing the union work because the people on the floor will need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened. More like a long road ahead with a clear sign at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Dani's bus job still be there at the end of that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robot driving comes around 2039 on this card, so no, probably not forever. That's the bit that worries me, both of us changing at the same time in our forties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy a flat in this one. Why here and not in the faster ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because ten years is long enough that a mortgage feels like a home, not a trap. In the two-year one I'd never sign for a mortgage, not with both our jobs in the air.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuse** for throwing anyone on the scrapheap.
I'd push for a **national retraining fund** paid for by the firms that profit.
think: Ten years means I'd be **thirty-seven** when thinking work goes, young enough to start again.
The real worry is **Dani's bus job** going around 2039, both of us changing together.
do: Keep the phone job for a few years and start a **gas or plumbing apprenticeship** in my early thirties.
Save for a **flat deposit** with Dani before prices shift.
Keep doing the **union rep** work for the people on the floor.
feel: **Uneasy** but not frightened, like a long road with a clear sign at the end.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that a mortgage feels like a home, not a trap.
fieldNote: Time changes his **money decisions** most: a mortgage becomes thinkable only here.
He still expects to **leave the phones**, so his income is at risk even with a decade.
His worry shifts to the **household**, with Dani's job also exposed later.

steps.text: Start a gas or plumbing apprenticeship in his early thirties
Save for a flat deposit with Dani
Keep representing the call floor as union rep

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. It's the speed, not the end point. What would help is a law that says firms can't just switch off a contact centre without paying for people to retrain, and a union that's at the table before the decision, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who answers the phone when the bot gets it wrong. A bot can set up a direct debit. A bot can't hear when someone on the hardship line is about to cry. Someone has to, and right now it's people like me on the hardship line. I'd want someone to remember that before they cut us all.

headlineQuote: A bot can set up a direct debit. A bot can't hear when someone on the hardship line is about to cry.
portrait: Rafael is a **27-year-old** senior agent on a water company's billing and hardship line, and the floor's **union rep**.
He never uses AI tools and closes the **suggested-reply box** on principle.
He sees every scenario through **staffing**: who gets cut, who gets retrained, who decides.
In the AGI pictures he plans a move into **plumbing or leak repair**, buying about three more years.
Only the ten-year picture lets him imagine a **mortgage** with his partner Dani, a bus driver.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because two years is too short to retrain properly.
whatWouldHelp: A **law** making firms pay for retraining before closing a contact centre.
The **union** at the table before decisions are made, not after.
